newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran's bid for zone of influence suffers setbacks.
newsitem.headline: Iran's bid for zone of influence suffers setbacks.

text.p: Iran's bid for regional influence has taken a battering with setbacks on both its eastern and western borders, religious concerns in Central Asia, and a U.S. military buildup in the Gulf, analysts said on Tuesday.
On all fronts, the Islamic republic of 60 million people ruled by Moslem clergymen is locked in an ideological battle for the hearts and minds of its neighbours.
"Their quest for regional influence has taken a bit of a battering lately. They're having to fight quite hard for it," one Middle East analyst said.

In the east, Tehran's Shi'ite Moslem rulers oppose the Taleban movement of radical Sunni Moslems who seized the Afghan capital Kabul last month from the government of Burhanuddin Rabbani, which Iran continues to recognise as legitimate.
Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati said the Taleban takeover posed a national security concern for Iran, "therefore, we cannot remain indifferent towards it".
In the Kyrgyzstan capital Bishkek, Velayati on Monday blamed foreign intervention for prolonging the Afghan conflict.
Iranian media have condemned the fundamentalist Taleban as manipulated by the United States, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia.
Afghanistan's new rulers accuse Iran of continuing to provoke the Taleban despite assurances relations would improve.
Leading Iranian clerics have described the Taleban as un-Islamic, sanctimonious and a disgrace to the religion.
On its western border, Iran is accused by a Kurdish faction in Iraq of helping a rival group to retake Iraq's biggest Kurdish city.
Iran has denied helping the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) retake Sulaimaniya from the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) backed by Baghdad who had occupied it for the last month.
Iran says its occasional intrusions into northern Iraq, such as an attack in July, targeted Iranian Kurdish rebels there.
Recent advances in Afghanistan and in northern Iraq by sides favoured by Iran may point to Tehran gaining advantage by refraining from hasty moves in the volatile region.
Advances by forces of the ousted Afghan government and the PUK's re-capture of Sulaimaniya and may restore some of Iran's lost influence.

Washington has urged the Kurds to steer clear of support from either Iran or Iraq, who ended an eight-year war in 1988, as part of the U.S. "dual containment" policy aimed at keeping either of them from gaining an upper hand in regional disputes.

To the south, Iran's Arab neighbours across the Gulf earlier this year charged Tehran with interference in their internal affairs, notably in the state of Bahrain where dissidents among the majority Shi'ite Moslem community oppose their Sunni rulers.
The United States has mounted a large military force in the strategic waterway, ostensibly to deter Iraqi President Saddam Hussein from threatening Kuwait.
And to Iran's north, Velayati and other envoys from Tehran are frequent visitors to neighbouring Turkmenistan and other former Soviet republics of Central Asia with large Islamic communities.
Iran has offered to use its influence to restart peace talks between the Russian-backed Tajikistan government and the armed Islamic opposition fighting a four-year civil war.
"The Taleban's sweep through Afghanistan was an indication that it didn't matter who the Iranians were backing, they didn't count," the Middle East analyst said.
"The Russian-CIS reaction to the Taleban is another indication of just how fearful they are of anything religious creeping into Central Asia.
"On the Iraq front, Iran didn't come out at all well in the previous round when the PUK lost control of Sulaimaniya.
"And the message from the Gulf Arabs to Washington seems to have been 'You really have got to stop debilitating Iraq because we're much more worried about Iran.'
"The only relatively quiescent place on Iran's borders, if you count the United States and its allies in the Gulf, is Armenia."
